notes: Fixed evaluation set for Aria's published error bars. 24 answers = 12 representative interview questions, each with one deliberately weak and one deliberately strong answer so the agreement statistics have real spread. Answers are written for the benchmark, not transcribed from real candidates, and the weak/strong labels are assigned by the same team that wrote the rubric. The 'quality' field IS the basis of the discrimination AUC in error-bars.json (see backend/errorbars.py: 257-258) - that test is therefore internally consistent rather than independent, and it is labelled a regression test, not a validation result. No human ratings have been collected; the candidate using Aria is never asked to grade it. Agreement with the independent judge model (llama3.2:3b) is kappa 0.33, reported as a limitation in the caveats.

answers.question: Tell me about a time you owned a project end to end.
answers.answer: I was part of a team that launched a feature. We worked on it for a while and it went live. It was a good experience and I learned a lot from the team.

answers.question: Tell me about a time you owned a project end to end.
answers.answer: I owned the checkout reliability workstream end to end. I set the error-budget policy, ran the weekly review, and rewrote the retry layer myself. That cut failed payments by 38% over a quarter, and I presented the post-mortem to the payments org.

answers.question: Describe a time you had to prioritise under a tight deadline.
answers.answer: I just tried to do everything at once and worked late. Some things slipped but we managed in the end. I think prioritising is important.

answers.question: Describe a time you had to prioritise under a tight deadline.
answers.answer: Two days before a release I had a P1 bug, a compliance deadline and a blocked mentee. I ranked by customer impact and irreversibility: I took the P1 myself, moved compliance to a teammate who had the context, and gave the mentee a smaller unblocked task. We shipped on time and I fixed the P1 in four hours.

answers.question: Tell me about a conflict with a teammate and how you resolved it.
answers.answer: There was some disagreement with a coworker but we talked about it and it was fine afterwards. I generally try to avoid conflict because it is not productive.

answers.question: Tell me about a conflict with a teammate and how you resolved it.
answers.answer: A senior engineer and I disagreed on whether notifications should use a queue or a cron job. I asked us each to write down our concerns, then scored both options against latency and ops cost. The queue won on the stated requirements, so I said so, and we adopted his retry design. We later co-authored the migration.

answers.question: Give an example of a time you failed and what you learned.
answers.answer: I once made a mistake and it was not great. But I moved on and things got better. I always try to do my best and learn from whatever happens.

answers.question: Give an example of a time you failed and what you learned.
answers.answer: I shipped a caching change that served stale prices to about 2,000 users. I missed a cache-invalidation path in review. I rolled it back in 20 minutes, wrote the post-mortem, and added an integration test and a canary rule for that class of change. I now treat invalidation as the risky half of any cache design.

answers.question: Walk me through a technical decision you made and the trade-offs.
answers.answer: I chose a database for the project because it seemed like the popular choice. It worked fine for what we needed. There are probably other options too but this one was okay.

answers.question: Walk me through a technical decision you made and the trade-offs.
answers.answer: For the audit log I chose append-only Postgres over Kafka. Kafka handled 10x the throughput, but we needed sub-second ad-hoc queries by user and team, and a Kafka read model would have doubled the operational surface. Postgres held our 3k writes per second with headroom, so I picked it and documented the throughput ceiling that would force a revisit.

answers.question: How do you make sure your work is clear to non-technical stakeholders?
answers.answer: I send updates and explain things in simple terms. If people have questions they can ask me. Communication is really important in a team.

answers.question: How do you make sure your work is clear to non-technical stakeholders?
answers.answer: I write a one-paragraph plain-language summary before any technical detail: what changes for the customer, when, and what could go wrong. For the billing migration I sent a two-line weekly update with a risk flag and a decision date. By week three the finance lead could describe the rollout to her own team without me in the room.

answers.question: Why are you interested in this role?
answers.answer: I am looking for a new opportunity and your company is a good company. I think I would be a good fit and I need a job where I can grow.

answers.question: Why are you interested in this role?
answers.answer: I have spent two years making internal developer tooling faster, and your posting is about exactly that at a larger scale. Your public docs mention a push to cut build times in half; I did that once for our monorepo and I want to do it where thousands of engineers feel it. The on-call rotation also matches how I like to work.

answers.question: Tell me about a time you collaborated across teams.
answers.answer: I worked with another team on a shared thing. We had meetings and it went okay. Collaboration with other teams is something I am comfortable with.

answers.question: Tell me about a time you collaborated across teams.
answers.answer: Payments needed a signed webhook from the identity team, and neither team's roadmap had room. I wrote a one-page interface contract with retry and idempotency rules, got both tech leads to sign it, and we built each side in parallel. The integration took half a day instead of the two weeks we had budgeted.

answers.question: Describe a situation where requirements were ambiguous.
answers.answer: The requirements were not very clear so I waited for someone to clarify them. Eventually the manager explained what he wanted. I just did what I was told after that.

answers.question: Describe a situation where requirements were ambiguous.
answers.answer: The brief said 'make search better' with no metric. I wrote down three candidate interpretations, estimated each, and sent them to the product lead in one message. He confirmed relevance and speed mattered most. I shipped a scoped version in two sprints and measured click-through, which went from 12% to 19%.

answers.question: How do you handle critical feedback?
answers.answer: I take feedback well and I do not get upset. If someone tells me something I try to fix it. I think I am pretty open to criticism.

answers.question: How do you handle critical feedback?
answers.answer: My lead told me my design docs were too long and buried the decision. It stung, but he was right. I rewrote two docs with the recommendation and risks in the first paragraph, and asked him to check the next one. He stopped commenting on length after that, and I now write the decision first by habit.

answers.question: Tell me about a time you improved a process or a metric.
answers.answer: I improved some parts of the process where I could. Things got a little better and the team seemed happier. I think continuous improvement is important.

answers.question: Tell me about a time you improved a process or a metric.
answers.answer: Our deploy pipeline took 42 minutes and engineers batched changes to avoid it. I profiled the build, cached the dependency layer, and parallelised the test shards. Deploy time dropped to 11 minutes and daily deploys went from about 3 to 14. I wrote up the change so the platform team could keep improving it.

answers.question: How would you debug a slow API endpoint?
answers.answer: I would look at the code and see if something is slow. Maybe add some logs. Then I would try to fix whatever looks wrong and test again.

answers.question: How would you debug a slow API endpoint?
answers.answer: First I confirm where the time goes: trace the request and compare p50 against p99 to separate a steady cost from a tail problem. If it is the database I check the query plan for a missing index or an N+1. For our orders endpoint that was an N+1 across line items; batching it cut p99 from 1.9s to 220ms.
